items.title: Le sfide dei nuovi sindaci socialisti negli Stati Uniti
items.summary: Da Los Angeles a Washington, la sinistra è andata al potere promettendo servizi e case più accessibili. L’obiettivo è dare risposte concrete e consolidare il consenso Leggi
items.content:
Le elezioni del 3 novembre hanno rafforzato la presenza della sinistra socialista alla guida delle città statunitensi. A Los Angeles Nithya Raman ha sconfitto la sindaca uscente Karen Bass, mentre a Washington ha vinto, come da pronostico, Janeese Lewis George. Le loro vittorie confermano una tendenza emersa nel 2025 con l’elezione di Zohran Mamdani a New York e Katie Wilson a Seattle. In campagna elettorale tutti questi politici hanno promesso di abbassare i prezzi degli alloggi e dei servizi essenziali, ma per riuscirci devono trovare finanziamenti, conquistare l’appoggio di altre istituzioni e superare divisioni anche tra i propri sostenitori.

A Los Angeles la questione principale sarà la casa. Raman, urbanista e consigliera comunale, appartiene ai Democratic socialists of America (Dsa), l’organizzazione socialista (di cui fa parte anche Mamdani) che negli ultimi anni è diventata molto influente a sinistra, riuscendo a far vincere le primarie del Partito democratico ai suoi militanti. Il suo programma combina il sostegno alla costruzione di nuove abitazioni con il controllo degli affitti e la protezione degli inquilini. L’obiettivo è aumentare l’offerta per contenere i prezzi, tutelando nel frattempo chi rischia di non riuscire più a pagare il canone.

Come spiega Marina Bolotnikova su Vox , questo approccio cerca di avvicinare posizioni spesso contrapposte nella sinistra statunitense. Raman sostiene che per affrontare la carenza di alloggi sia necessario facilitare anche l’attività dei costruttori privati. Allo stesso tempo, ha contribuito alla riforma approvata nel 2025 che ha introdotto limiti più severi agli aumenti annuali degli affitti negli appartamenti per cui valgono le tutele comunali. Gli aumenti oggi sono legati all’inflazione e non possono superare il 4 per cento .

Il piano di Raman richiede di ripensare profondamente una città molto estesa e dipendente dalle automobili, dove circa tre quarti dei terreni residenziali sono riservati alle case unifamiliari. Per costruire edifici con più appartamenti in questi quartieri, bisogna superare l’opposizione dei proprietari che vogliono solo case singole. Anche Bass aveva introdotto una procedura accelerata per autorizzare progetti destinati ad alloggi a prezzi accessibili, ma dopo le proteste aveva escluso queste zone. Il programma aveva comunque avviato la costruzione di migliaia di appartamenti.

Le resistenze vengono anche da una parte della sinistra. A gennaio Raman aveva proposto di modificare la Measure Ula, una tassa sulle vendite degli immobili più costosi che finanzia alloggi a prezzi accessibili e aiuti agli inquilini a rischio di perdere la casa. Voleva introdurre esenzioni per i costruttori, sostenendo che il prelievo scoraggiasse la realizzazione di nuovi edifici con più appartamenti. Le associazioni per la casa si erano opposte, temendo di perdere risorse necessarie a prevenire gli sfratti, e Raman aveva ritirato la proposta.

Per capire come le promesse di Raman potranno tradursi in decisioni di governo, molti guardano al caso di New York. Sul Los Angeles Times , Jenny Jarvie ha spiegato che nei primi dieci mesi di mandato Mamdani ha cominciato ad attuare il suo programma per ridurre le spese delle famiglie, ma ha incontrato ostacoli sulle misure che richiedono l’accordo del governo statale.

A giugno la commissione che stabilisce gli aumenti per gli appartamenti ad affitto regolamentato ha votato il blocco dei canoni per i rinnovi dei contratti di uno e due anni. È una delle principali promesse mantenute da Mamdani, anche se riguarda solo gli alloggi coperti da queste tutele.

Grazie a un accordo con la governatrice dello stato di New York Kathy Hochul (anche lei del Partito democratico ma di orientamento moderato), il comune ha inoltre cominciato a offrire posti gratuiti nei servizi educativi per i bambini di due anni . Ha anche esteso a più famiglie a basso reddito gli aiuti per pagare l’asilo nido e gli altri servizi per l’infanzia. E a ottobre ha annunciato che avrebbe gradualmente esteso questi aiuti alle famiglie di più di diecimila bambini in lista d’attesa. In campagna elettorale Mamdani aveva promesso di garantire servizi gratuiti a tutti i bambini sotto i cinque anni, ma per riuscirci serviranno altri posti e finanziamenti.

Su altre proposte l’accordo con lo stato non è arrivato. Come ha ricostruito City & State , Hochul si è opposta agli aumenti delle imposte sui redditi più alti e sulle grandi società, con cui Mamdani vuole finanziare i nuovi servizi. Il sindaco non può introdurli senza l’autorizzazione statale. Resta da realizzare anche la promessa di rendere gratuiti gli autobus di linea, una proposta che incontra le resistenze della governatrice e dei vertici dell’ente statale che gestisce il servizio.

Dopo le elezioni, Hochul ha aperto alla possibilità di aumentare le entrate fiscali per finanziare i servizi per l’infanzia, senza impegnarsi ad approvare le imposte proposte da Mamdani. Bisogna quindi da stabilire come sostenere nel tempo le nuove spese e allargare l’accesso ai servizi.

Mamdani è comunque popolare tra i newyorchesi . In un sondaggio della Suffolk University condotto all’inizio di settembre, il 57 per cento degli elettori registrati giudicava positivamente il suo lavoro e il 61 per cento riteneva che stesse facendo meglio del previsto.

A Seattle, invece, la sindaca Katie Wilson sta perdendo consensi. In un sondaggio condotto ad agosto da Fulcrum strategy group per la camera di commercio locale, il 37 per cento degli elettori registrati esprimeva un’opinione favorevole sulla sindaca, contro il 57 per cento di aprile.

Una delle principali ragioni della sfiducia è la sicurezza: solo un terzo degli intervistati riteneva che l’amministrazione avesse un piano efficace per migliorarla. Come racconta l’emittente pubblica locale Knkx , il sondaggio è arrivato nel pieno del dibattito sull’uso delle telecamere di sorveglianza, sostenute dalla camera di commercio e contestate dagli attivisti per la tutela della privacy. Wilson deve quindi rispondere alla richiesta di interventi più incisivi sulla sicurezza senza ignorare le preoccupazioni di una parte della sua base.

A complicare il suo compito ci sono le difficoltà finanziarie del comune. Per i prossimi due anni Wilson ha proposto tagli alla spesa , cercando tuttavia di aumentare i posti nei centri per le persone senza dimora e di rafforzare la polizia. Vorrebbe finanziare i servizi anche con nuove imposte progressive, che però non potranno entrare in vigore abbastanza presto da coprire il disavanzo attuale.

A Washington, Janeese Lewis George dovrà affrontare vincoli ancora più stringenti. Ha promesso maggiori tutele per gli inquilini , investimenti nei servizi per l’infanzia e modifiche alle regole che limitano la costruzione di abitazioni. Per finanziarli ha prospettato aumenti delle imposte sulle imprese e sui residenti più ricchi, che richiederanno il sostegno del consiglio comunale.

La capitale, però, è un distretto federale con un’autonomia locale limitata : il congresso può bloccare le leggi cittadine e intervenire sul bilancio. Da gennaio i democratici avranno la maggioranza sia alla camera sia al senato. La sindaca potrebbe quindi trovare interlocutori più favorevoli alle sue politiche, ma i suoi margini d’azione resteranno ridotti.

Anche sul piano finanziario ci sono dei vincoli. La città deve mantenere il bilancio in pareggio: per ampliare i servizi per l’infanzia e gli aiuti agli inquilini, Lewis George dovrà convincere il consiglio comunale ad aumentare le entrate oppure trovare risorse riducendo altre spese.

Internazionale pubblica ogni settimana una pagina di lettere. Ci piacerebbe sapere cosa pensi di questo articolo. Scrivici a: posta@internazionale.it

items.title: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS
items.summary: I grew up with Black Ops 2 and wanted to see if I could make it work on my 2020 MacBook Pro. So I used Claude Opus 5.5 to create a tool that converts your copy of the game (from Steam) to a native ARM64 Mac app, with almost 60fps in all areas. The whole game is statically recompilated ahead-of-time (AOT) and does not use any emulator whatsoever, be it Wine, Crossover or Rosetta. The best thing is the performance, although some heat issues are still to fix. You get to play the whole Campaign, local Multiplayer (with bots) and local Zombies (all DLCs maps; you need to have them in your Steam lib
items.content:
Call of Duty: Black Ops II, statically recompiled from 32-bit x86 Windows to native ARM64 macOS. Campaign, Zombies and multiplayer against bots, built on your Mac from your own Steam copy.

Why · Abstract · Method · Limits · Repository · Legal Beta, 2026-11-03 · measured on one Apple M1 (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores, 16 GB)

Campaign (Angola), Zombies (Town) and multiplayer (Hijacked, against bots) on an Apple M1, recorded while playing; the number in the top right corner is frames per second, and the screen recording itself costs some, mostly in the campaign. 80-second video (MP4, 20 MB)

This repository contains no game file and no translated game code. It turns your own Steam copy of Black Ops II into an app for your Mac, on your Mac. The game's code ends up inside that app, so nobody can hand you a ready-made one: each player builds their own, and it may not be shared. Unofficial fan project, not affiliated with Activision, Treyarch or Microsoft. To play, buy the game. Beta: read what has and has not been proven .

Black Ops II never came out on Mac, and on Apple Silicon it was not really playable before. AppleGamingWiki lists it as unplayable under CrossOver and not supported under Rosetta 2. What remains is a Windows ARM virtual machine in Parallels, with reports ranging from 1 frame per second in matches on an M1 Max to 60–80 on M3 and M4 ( MacGamingDB ). Here the game is translated once, before it starts, into a native ARM64 app: 51–60 frames per second on a base M1, with no Windows and no virtual machine. Being native also means it can be fixed and extended like any Mac app: split-screen, which the PC version never had, is in progress.

bo2-mac takes the three executables of Black Ops II, the campaign ( t6sp.exe ), Zombies ( t6zm.exe ) and multiplayer ( t6mp.exe ), and turns their x86 machine code into ARM64 machine code ahead of time. Remill lifts each function to LLVM IR, a chain of our own passes rewrites that IR, and the result is linked with a Win32 runtime written by hand, whose Direct3D 11 is drawn by Metal. There is no Wine and no JIT: the game runs as native code, in one process. About 150,000 functions are translated across the three executables. Only the short sequences that the copy protection hides run in a small x86 interpreter, and so does any code the translation missed, so a hole is built to cost speed rather than crash the game.

On an Apple M1 the campaign runs at 51–60 frames per second , and every mission loads and hands over to the next one, down to the end credits. Zombies is played solo on six maps through the game's own menus at 57–60 . Multiplayer is played against bots through its real menus, eleven game modes, at 53–60 . One app, Black Ops II.app , opens the campaign, and the CAMPAIGN / ZOMBIES / MULTIPLAYER entries of each menu switch to the other game.

Nothing is downloaded from anyone but you: the converter reads the executables of the copy you bought, checks them byte for byte, and builds the app on your machine.

Frame rate counts the drawables really presented to the screen, checked against the screen and the Metal HUD.

All three modes: keyboard and mouse, or a DualSense as XInput through GameController.framework; sound on; movement keys follow their position on your keyboard (ZQSD on AZERTY, WASD on QWERTY), unless you bound them yourself in the game's options.

The copy protection is executed, not bypassed. The game hides integrity checks behind hardware exceptions, single-step traps and code it decrypts into the heap. A small x86 machine built on Unicorn ( x86_guest_vm.cpp , heap_code.cpp ) runs exactly those sequences and hands control back to the recompiled code. No check result is forced and no key is placed by hand.

A hole in the translation is built to cost speed, not a crash. When the game reaches x86 code that was never lifted, the same machine runs its original bytes ( interp.cpp ) and gives control back to the recompiled code at the next translated block, call or return. Each interpreted address is logged ( [INTERP] ).

The online service is answered locally. Zombies and multiplayer expect Demonware; a responder written from the game's own requests ( dw_local.cpp ) answers the lobby, storage and ticket on your Mac. Nothing leaves the machine.

They translate Windows calls at run time and keep the x86 code under Rosetta. Here the x86 code itself is gone: it is ARM64 machine code before the game starts. DXVK and DXMT are PE DLLs that reach their native backend through Wine's unixlib mechanism; this port has no Wine, and its Direct3D 11 is its own layer over 32-bit guest memory. Only shader translation was needed from outside, and HLSLcc, a plain C++ library, covers it.

Each entry is a symptom seen on screen, the cause that was measured, and the effect of the fix.

F1 · The lifter ignored the x87 rounding mode. In Zombies the prone view shook. fistp rounded to nearest where the game had asked for truncation, inside the network codec of the view height. The height received by the client was wrong on 8 samples out of 8, and on 0 out of 8 after a Remill patch and a re-lift of the codec.

F2 · One reserved bit of the x87 control word. A campaign mission froze in an effects loop, only with real threads. The lifter stored bit 6 of the control word differently from real hardware. A one-line Remill patch and four re-lifted runtime functions fixed it, with no slowdown.

F3 · A CPU feature flag changes the algorithm. Our IsProcessorFeaturePresent answered "no SSE2", so the C runtime took its x87 ceil , which rounded to nearest under our runtime. An effect then sampled index −1 forever: two missions froze.

F4 · Our own log caused the stutter. Hitches of 170–430 ms were the render thread blocked in write() : our log, redirected to a file on a nearly full disk. Sending it through a pipe to a child process took the hitches per run from 12 and 8 to 0 and 0.

F5 · Shader translation moved constants by 4 bytes. HLSLcc placed a float2 after a float at offset 24 where Direct3D reads it at 20. 31 of 2,664 shaders were affected, among them the eyes and the reticles.

F6 · The protection has to run. The options menu froze 8 times out of 8. An integrity check rewrites its own return address to point at code decrypted into the heap, which the runtime ignored. Running that code, as Windows does, gave 3 out of 3 without a freeze.

F7 · Our own safety guards were the obstacle. One guard of ours stopped the game at 28 seconds of play. The largest gains of the project came from removing our own guards and false sharing, not from clever code.

F8 · An empty API stub looks like a broken service. Two stubs that returned nothing ( CryptGenRandom , StringFromGUID2 ) looked like a network failure in Zombies.

F9 · Thread priorities are part of the program. SetThreadPriority was a stub. Passing the mixer's request to macOS cut the short audio buffers of a run from 908–1872 to 7–71, and the sound gaps with them.

F10 · Native skinning, bit for bit. CPU skinning rewritten in NEON gives the same bits as the original x86 and took a heavy scene from 17.8 to 30.3 fps.

F11 · Decals need the game's depth bias. Scorch marks and blood appeared or vanished with a slight turn of the camera. The game asks for a depth bias on decals; our layer left it at zero. Passing the game's values to Metal fixed it.

F12 · The render thread was copying the level's geometry every frame. In multiplayer and Zombies it copied 23–63 MB of vertex data to the GPU per frame, most of it static. Keeping static buffers resident in Metal brought the copies to 3.5–5 MB per frame: multiplayer 51.8 → 60 fps, Zombies 43.1 → 58.2. The same change does nothing in the campaign, where the pace is set by the scheduler thread. A speed-up helps only the mode whose bottleneck it touches.

F13 · A false start inside one instruction cost half the frame rate in combat. In the first conversions from a fresh Steam copy, Zombies fell to 25 fps whenever the player fired. Hot functions were running in the interpreter: the catalogue placed the start of the next function inside the first instruction of a root, so its bounded sweep decoded zero bytes and the root was dropped without a word. Sweeping such roots without the bound, as the one-by-one lifter already did, put them back in the translated code.

Deterministic record and replay. With every guest thread a coroutine on one host thread, most sources of non-determinism are gone; the replay is checked against the recording, not assumed. Three boundaries capture all outside input: the import dispatcher, the window message drain, and the consumed audio buffers. The journal is about 16 MB. It allows the same run twice with exactly one flag changed.

The instrument is the thing that fails. Nearly 200 findings were taken back along the way. The largest share (31%) were an instrument that answered a different question; the next (17%), one that could not answer at all. So every oracle here names its input and refuses to answer when that input is missing.

Clean room for the match rules. Multiplayer and Zombies take their match rules from a daily patch file that Steam no longer ships. The replacement in runtime/match_rules/ was written by a team that never saw the original script: one team wrote a behavioural specification from the game, the other wrote the code from that specification alone, and the two only spoke through written questions and answers, kept with their dates.

items.title: Gli album da ascoltare
items.summary: Da Burning song di Kali Malone a Rooming house di Charlie Parr. Le recensioni della stampa straniera Leggi
items.content:
Nel 2023 con Does spring hide its joy Kali Malone, il chitarrista dei Sunn O))) Stephen O’Malley e Lucy Railton dilatavano singoli accordi fino a dimensioni monumentali, trasformando minime variazioni timbriche in un’esperienza immersiva. Con Burning song Malone torna all’organo, ma abbandona le vaste architetture sonore del passato per composizioni più brevi, intime e ricche di melodie. Registrato nella chiesa di San Tommaso a Lipsia, dove riposa Johann Sebastian Bach, l’album intreccia l’organo alla chitarra acustica suonata con l’archetto di O’Malley e al violoncello di Railton. I tre strumenti si fondono fino a perdere la propria identità creando un paesaggio sonoro sospeso, in cui conta più la relazione tra i suoni che la loro origine. Brani come Map the path e Crawling ashore evocano paesaggi, movimenti e fragili approdi emotivi. Attraversato da un senso di perdita e inquietudine, Burning song conserva tuttavia una tensione verso il futuro. Le sue melodie si rincorrono senza trovare una vera quiete, mentre la conclusiva My eve my dawn suggerisce che ogni fine contiene già un nuovo inizio. Un disco elegiaco e luminoso, che trasforma il dolore in una domanda aperta: “E adesso?”. Sasha Geffen, Pitchfork

Sembra un disco scritto per il presente, segnato dalla difficoltà di accedere alle cure mediche, dalla solidarietà tra vicini e dalla precarietà abitativa. Eppure Rooming house , la nuova “opera folk” di Charlie Parr, dimostra quanto la sua musica, apparentemente fuori dal tempo, sia ancora attuale. “Le mie canzoni nascono quasi sempre dalle mie esperienze o da quelle delle persone che mi circondano”, racconta il cantautore e chitarrista blues e folk, sessantenne di Saint Paul. “E oggi molte persone stanno vivendo momenti terribili”. Diventato uno dei musicisti del Minnesota più conosciuti anche all’estero, Parr ha costruito una carriera raccontando povertà, sofferenza e difficoltà quotidiane. Più che adattarsi al presente, è il presente ad aver tristemente raggiunto il suo universo narrativo. Pubblicato dall’etichetta senza scopo di lucro Smithsonian Folkways, Rooming house affronta problemi che sembravano destinati a risolversi e invece continuano ad aggravarsi: l’accesso alla sanità, la mancanza di alloggi dignitosi, l’insicurezza economica. Cresciuto ascoltando Woody Guthrie, Lead Belly e l’ Anthology of American folk music di Harry Smith, Parr si è formato anche attraverso la scena folk e blues di Minneapolis degli anni sessanta, la stessa che influenzò Bob Dylan. Tra i suoi riferimenti ci sono Dave Ray, Tony Glover e Spider John Koerner, che nel 2022 gli ha regalato la sua chitarra. Chris Riemenschneider, Minnesota Star Tribune

L’orchestra della radio di Vienna diretta da Simone Menezes ci offre un programma molto ordinato: tre lavori neo­classici pieni dello spirito di Haydn e Mozart. La sinfonia detta “classica” di Prokofev ha una discografia ricchissima, ma gli altri due lavori sono molto più rari. La sinfonietta di Francis Poulenc si rifà a Haydn, ma è molto concreta: l’allegro con fuoco iniziale è gestito con energia e c’è un brio molto parigino negli archi. Menezes gestisce bene i fulminei cambiamenti d’umore di tutto il lavoro, forse solo il finale è un po’ pesante. Sottotitolata In memoria di Mozart , la sinfonietta di Heitor Villa-Lobos pare che sia ispirata da Le nozze di Figaro . Fa piacere incontrare una musicista brasiliana che sostiene con questi ottimi risultati la causa del suo compatriota. Il lavoro di Villa-Lobos è stato scritto nel 1917 come quello di Prokofev, che purtroppo qui riceve un’esecuzione un po’ piatta: solo la Gavotte ha la leggerezza che manca al resto. Gli altri due pezzi rari sono comunque un’ottima consolazione. Mark Pullinger, Gramophone

items.title: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave
items.summary: Article URL: https://gatezh.com/posts/macos-secure-enclave-ssh-keys/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50449748 Points: 303 # Comments: 109
items.content:
I've been paranoid about my SSH keys for a while now. They just sit there in ~/.ssh/ , protected by nothing but file permissions. Any malicious script that gets access to my filesystem could just copy them and get into all my servers. Also, there have been many stories out there online about fake interview assignments that asked to clone a repo and run it on your local machine. This is one of the reasons I switched completely to using devcontainers, but even that was not really enough for me (and it shouldn't be enough for you or anybody else really).

I have decided to NOT go with the native macOS Secure Enclave approach (using only out-of-the-box tools) because it ended up plain ugly and I can't live with that. However, it is a fully functional, working solution that I would definitely use otherwise.

After some research, I found several ways to protect SSH keys:

I already use 1Password, but I might switch to something else in the future. Bitwarden recently added SSH key support (even on the free tier!), but it's still a software solution — the keys are encrypted at rest but decrypted in memory when used.

What I really wanted was hardware-backed security. The private key should literally be impossible to extract, even if my Mac is fully compromised.

That left me with YubiKey or Secure Enclave. I have a YubiKey 5C, but I wanted to try the native approach first — no extra hardware to carry around, no third-party apps to maintain.

Since macOS Sequoia (and Tahoe), macOS supports SSH keys backed by the Secure Enclave, a security subsystem on the Mac's chip that is isolated from the main processor. The private key is created inside it and never leaves.

When you SSH somewhere, your Mac asks the Secure Enclave to sign the authentication challenge. If you enable Touch ID, you have to approve each signing operation. The actual private key never exists in memory or on disk.

macOS provides the sc_auth command (Smart Card Authentication) to manage CryptoTokenKit identities. Despite the name, it works with Secure Enclave too.

Turns out my Touch ID enrollment got reset somehow. After re-enrolling my fingerprint in System Settings → Touch ID & Password , the command worked fine.

Now we need to create a "key handle" file that SSH can use. This is NOT the private key — it's just a reference that tells SSH "go ask the Secure Enclave to sign this."

When prompted for PIN, just press Enter (it's not used for biometric keys). Touch ID will pop up. This creates id_ecdsa_sk_rk and id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub in your current directory.

If you search for "macOS Secure Enclave SSH" online, you'll find a lot of guides telling you to run ssh-add -K . Don't. It's deprecated:

And even the new flags don't work for Secure Enclave keys — they're for the traditional macOS Keychain, not CryptoTokenKit. The SSH_SK_PROVIDER environment variable is the correct approach.

That ssh: at the end is the FIDO2 application ID — it's part of the key, not a comment. You can add your own comment after it when copying to authorized_keys :

Or manually paste the public key (with your comment) into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.

After setting everything up, I tried to SSH… and it asked for my password.

The verbose output ( ssh -vvv ) showed SSH was only trying my old RSA key:

The problem: SSH doesn't automatically look for files named id_ecdsa_sk_rk . It only auto-discovers standard names like id_rsa , id_ed25519 , id_ecdsa .

SSH tries identity files in order, so put the Secure Enclave key first if you want it to be the default.

⚠️ Note: If you're using 1Password's SSH agent ( IdentityAgent ), it might conflict with this setup. I had to comment it out while testing.

One thing I'm not thrilled about: the Touch ID dialog says "ctccardtoken needs to authenticate to continue" instead of something friendly like "SSH wants to use your key."

This is because the prompt comes from CryptoTokenKit — a low-level framework that Apple hasn't polished for end-user SSH. If this bothers you, Secretive provides a much nicer UI while still using Secure Enclave under the hood.

I initially thought about creating two keys — one with Touch ID for "important" servers, one without for convenience (like Git operations).

But then I realized: without -t bio , malware could use my key silently. With -t bio , I always know when something is using my SSH key. A few extra taps per day is a small price for that visibility.

So my recommendation if you're planning to store your SSH keys this way: just use -t bio for everything. If it ever gets annoying, you can always create a second key later.

Secure Enclave keys are tied to your specific Mac. If your Mac dies, the keys die with it.

That's by design: the key can't be exported, so it can't be backed up either. Keep more than one key instead. Add your Secure Enclave key AND a backup key (from a YubiKey, or another Mac) to your servers' authorized_keys . If one device is lost, you still have access via the other.

It seems to be a proper way to store your SSH keys securely, and it is way better than storing them on your hard drive.

However, I've been somewhat surprised by the ugliness of the UI. Not sure why Apple released such an unpolished thing. In each and every presentation they have a section on security (where their Apple logo becomes an Apple lock), so I was expecting an actual aesthetically appealing look for their security features. It is definitely not the case. My sense of beauty is not compatible with this ugliness, so I will be looking into other solutions to store my SSH keys in Secure Enclave such as Secretive .

I also still need a backup option in case anything happens to my Mac.

items.title: Gli insegnanti devono essere neutrali?
items.summary: In Germania due alunni hanno fatto una domanda sull’Afd al loro professore, e lui ha risposto. Da lì è nato un caso che ha diviso il paese Leggi
items.content:
Max Heckel insegna educazione tecnica e tedesco in una scuola secondaria di Stendal, una cittadina di 40mila abitanti nel nord della Sassonia-Anhalt, in Germania. Nell’ultimo anno è diventato un caso nazionale per alcune frasi pronunciate in classe sul partito di estrema destra Alternative für Deutschland (Afd). Il partito ha presentato un reclamo, l’ufficio scolastico regionale lo ha ammonito per aver violato l’obbligo di neutralità e lui ha fatto ricorso.

Abbiamo raccontato la sua storia la settimana scorsa con un articolo della Zeit. Ora c’è una novità: il 4 novembre, tre settimane prima dell’udienza in tribunale, il richiamo disciplinare è stato cancellato.

Ma la vicenda mostra bene cosa sta succedendo dentro e fuori le scuole tedesche, quindi vale la pena di ripercorrerla con l’aiuto di Anne Fromm, che l’ha ricostruita sulla Tageszeitung.

Nel parlamento della Sassonia-Anhalt il capogruppo e candidato di punta dell’Afd, Ulrich Siegmund , interviene a sostegno di una mozione del suo partito sulla neutralità politica a scuola. È un giorno di ottobre del 2025, mancano undici mesi alle elezioni nel land. Siegmund fa un esempio: “A Stendal c’è una scuola in cui lavora un insegnante di estrema sinistra”. L’Afd ha presentato un reclamo dopo la segnalazione di una madre, e Siegmund vuole sapere a che punto è (non dice che sua moglie fa parte del personale di quella scuola).

Il ministro dell’istruzione Jan Riedel, della Cdu, conferma: l’insegnante “ha preso chiaramente posizione contro l’Afd” e l’ufficio scolastico ha avviato un provvedimento disciplinare. In breve: il leader locale dell’estrema destra si lamenta in parlamento di un docente e il ministro dell’istruzione gli dà ragione.

L’episodio a cui fa riferimento il ministro risale al marzo 2025, una settimana dopo le elezioni per il rinnovo del Bundestag , il parlamento federale. Alla fine dell’ora di educazione tecnica due alunni di dodici anni chiedono a Heckel se ha votato per l’Afd.

Lui risponde di no e, visto che insistono, spiega perché: la politica fiscale del partito, che favorisce i più ricchi, l’idea di “remigrazione” discussa a Potsdam in un incontro a cui aveva partecipato anche Siegmund; il rifiuto delle politiche di inclusione. E gli mostra al computer alcuni materiali. Poi aggiunge che ognuno è libero di votare per l’Afd, ma chi lo fa dev’essere “molto ricco, privo di scrupoli morali o di buon senso”.

Secondo l’ufficio scolastico regionale, Heckel non ha aiutato gli alunni a formarsi un’opinione, ma ha cercato di imporre la sua. L’Afd sarebbe un tema troppo complesso per l’ora di educazione tecnica, e senza preparazione Heckel non poteva discutere “con la necessaria profondità oggettiva” della “cosiddetta remigrazione” (come se l’espulsione di massa fosse un tema da valutare con pro e contro).

Non è la prima volta che l’Afd prende di mira Heckel. Lo aveva già fatto nel 2021, anche sui social media, esponendolo a minacce di morte. Ma è la prima volta che l’ufficio scolastico regionale richiama un insegnante per alcune frasi sul partito (il sindacato Gew non conosce casi simili nel resto della Germania). E un richiamo disciplinare non è una formalità: alla violazione successiva si rischia il licenziamento.

Nell’ottobre 2025 l’ufficio propone a Heckel di cancellare il richiamo dal fascicolo dopo sei mesi. Lui rifiuta, perché vuole che un tribunale chiarisca cosa significa essere “neutrali”. L’udienza è fissata per il 27 novembre, ma il 4 novembre l’ufficio cancella il richiamo “per il tempo trascorso”, anche se secondo i giuristi consultati dalla Tageszeitung di solito un richiamo resta valido due o tre anni. Non ci sarà nessuna sentenza.

A Stendal, centro principale dell’Altmark, una zona rurale vicino all’Elba, alle elezioni per il parlamento federale del 2025 l’Afd ha preso il 37 per cento, e nella simulazione di voto organizzata nella scuola di Heckel il risultato è stato simile. Alle regionali del 6 settembre il partito ha ottenuto nel land il 43,8 per cento dei voti. Per cui l’insegnante è consapevole di come suonano le sue parole sull’Afd.

Ma bisogna anche guardare chi siede nelle classi. Circa un quarto degli studenti di Heckel è di origine straniera; molti fanno fatica a leggere e scrivere, o hanno disturbi del neurosviluppo; le famiglie spesso vivono di sussidi. E, come ovunque nella regione, mancano insegnanti: a farne le spese è stata anche l’ora di educazione civica, cancellata.

Il programma dell’Afd per l’istruzione colpirebbe ragazze e ragazzi come loro. Prevede classi separate per i figli di rifugiati e richiedenti asilo, la fine immediata dell’inclusione degli alunni con disabilità e un tetto per cui solo un quarto degli studenti potrebbe andare al liceo. Vuole l’istruzione domiciliare, servizi di vigilanza nelle scuole, la bandiera tedesca issata ogni giorno e più spazio in storia alla “nascita della nazione tedesca” e all’impero di Bismarck. E punta a sostituire l’agenzia regionale per l’educazione civica con un “istituto per l’educazione allo stato e all’identità culturale”.

Secondo gli esperti di diritto consultati dal sito Correctiv prima del voto nel land, alcune proposte, come la bandiera e i programmi, si potrebbero introdurre con una semplice circolare. Altre violerebbero la costituzione o il diritto internazionale.

E poi c’è la neutralità, usata sempre di più come arma politica . L’Afd sommerge l’ufficio scolastico di reclami e il parlamento d’interrogazioni. Un deputato del partito si è lamentato pubblicamente di una scuola perché il nome sapeva troppo di “ideologia arcobaleno”. L’istituto si chiama Quer-Bunt: Quer perché si trova a Querfurt, e bunt (variopinta) perché la facciata è colorata.

Tuttavia il Beutelsbacher Konsens , il documento che definisce come va fatta educazione civica in Germania, non parla di neutralità. Non è una legge, ma le sue indicazioni sono entrate nei regolamenti scolastici dei land e nelle sentenze dei tribunali.

Fu scritto nel 1976, in un clima di forte polarizzazione simile a quello di oggi: in quegli anni centinaia di insegnanti furono esclusi dal servizio pubblico o licenziati per le loro idee, e destra e sinistra temevano che la democrazia non reggesse. Il compromesso trovato a Beutelsbach fissa tre princìpi: gli studenti non devono essere indottrinati; ciò che è controverso nella scienza o nella politica va presentato come controverso; la scuola deve mettere ragazze e ragazzi nelle condizioni di esaminare la situazione politica e i propri interessi.

Michael Wrase, professore di diritto pubblico all’università di Hildesheim, ha ragionato sulla questione con la Zeit e con la Süddeutsche Zeitung .

Gli insegnanti devono essere neutrali rispetto all’Afd? No. Secondo Wrase, dal punto di vista giuridico non cambia nulla, neanche con l’Afd al governo: le affermazioni palesemente false o contrarie ai valori della costituzione vanno contestate. E una circolare che impone agli insegnanti di non esprimersi politicamente sarebbe illegittima, perché prevalgono la libertà d’espressione e il dovere di difendere la costituzione. “Il silenzio non è un’opzione”.

Possono dire in classe che chi vota Afd fa un grave errore? Sì, se lo inseriscono in una discussione. È vietato l’“indottrinamento unilaterale”, cioè dire che un partito è cattivo e basta. L’insegnante non deve tenere per sé la propria opinione e può anche ricordare che nel land l’Afd è classificata dai servizi segreti interni come un partito “estremista di destra accertato”.

E le spille o le magliette con la scritta “Fck Afd”? Non sono vietate in sé. Negli anni ottanta il tribunale federale del lavoro impedì a un insegnante d’indossare una spilla contro il nucleare perché la esibiva in modo “ostentato”, non per aprire una discussione.

Il criterio è sempre lo stesso: avviare un confronto è lecito, influenzare in modo unilaterale no. Per questo distribuire volantini contro l’Afd non è ammesso (perché il partito non è fuorilegge e ha diritto a essere trattato come gli altri), mentre invitare a partecipare a una manifestazione contro l’estremismo di destra sì.

Cosa succederebbe con l’Afd al governo? Il rischio è un clima di intimidazione: insegnanti che se ne vanno, famiglie che iscrivono i figli alle scuole private, istituti che si dividono tra isole progressiste e altre vicine all’Afd. Il partito non può cancellare le politiche per l’inclusione ma potrebbe svuotarle di significato, trasformando alcuni istituti in centri speciali per alunni con disabilità.

Inoltre un governo può incidere su una scuola anche senza cambiare le leggi: per esempio, tagliando i fondi a un progetto contro il razzismo. Wrase si aspetta però una “resistenza silenziosa” dei funzionari, con obiezioni giuridiche e tempi burocratici che si allungano.

Quanto al caso di Stendal, Wrase sostiene che Heckel abbia “agito correttamente” e il tribunale gli avrebbe probabilmente dato ragione (l’intervista della Zeit è di metà settembre, prima che il richiamo fosse cancellato). La sua conclusione è che gli insegnanti “non devono lasciarsi intimidire”.

items.title: Lo scandalo della Nvidia fa tremare il mondo delle ia
items.summary: Jensen Huang, amministratore delegato del colosso dei processori Nvidia, ha ammesso una relazione con Alice Huang, sospettata di essere una spia cinese Leggi
items.content:
Una delle aziende più importanti e ricche del mondo è sull’orlo di una crisi profonda e rischia di danneggiare il primato degli Stati Uniti in un settore ormai strategico come quello dell’intelligenza artificiale (ia) a causa di una relazione extraconiugale del suo fondatore e amministratore delegato.

L’8 novembre Jensen Huang, il carismatico amministratore delegato della Nvidia, il colosso statunitense al centro del boom dell’ia grazie ai suoi processori innovativi, ha ammesso di avere una relazione con una donna di nazionalità cinese, Alice Huang, sospettata di essere una spia al servizio di Pechino.

Il manager ha inviato una lettera ai dipendenti dell’azienda, scrivendo di dovere delle “scuse alla mia famiglia e a tutti voi. Ho tradito mia moglie. Il mio comportamento ha fatto del male a lei e ai nostri figli. Quello che ho fatto è imperdonabile. Mi dispiace profondamente”. In un comunicato la Nvidia ha reso noto di aver aperto “ un’inchiesta interna indipendente” per capire se Huang sia davvero finito al centro di un’operazione messa in piedi dai servizi segreti cinesi.

Lo scandalo è esploso sulla scia di una serie di rivelazioni fatte dalla stampa statunitense nei mesi scorsi. Al centro c’è la figura di Alice Huang . Per anni la donna avrebbe lavorato prima come reporter della tv di stato cinese e in seguito si sarebbe occupata di prodotti finanziari per alcune aziende, tra cui la banca britannica Hsbc.

Una svolta significativa della sua carriera è arrivata nel 2023, quando ha cominciato a dirigere la Megaspeed International, un’azienda con sede a Singapore nata come costola di un produttore di videogiochi cinese. La Megaspeed si presenta come una fornitrice di servizi cloud basati sui processori Nvidia per gli sviluppatori di intelligenze artificiali nella regione dell’Asia-Pacifico.

Dal novembre 2023 è partner ufficiale della Nvidia, uno status che le garantisce l’accesso ai suoi processori più avanzati. Tra i clienti della Megaspeed ci sono anche aziende tecnologiche cinesi – per esempio il colosso del commercio online Alibaba – che sono da sempre molto interessate ai chip della Nvidia ma non possono comprare quelli più avanzati a causa del divieto imposto dal governo statunitense.

Quando sia cominciata la relazione tra Jensen Huang e Alice Huang (stesso cognome, ma nessun legame di parentela) non è ancora chiaro, ma è certo che all’inizio del 2024 erano insieme a un evento organizzato dalla Nvidia in California. In quei giorni Alice dichiarava che “Jensen è un mio grande amico”.

In seguito i due sono stati visti in pubblico più volte: per esempio, nel giugno 2024 alla Computex Taipei , una delle fiere tecnologiche più importanti del mondo, e l’anno dopo, sempre a Taiwan, in un ristorante della capitale insieme ad altri manager. In varie foto e video circolati in quei giorni erano spesso “guancia a guancia” e andavano via insieme nella stessa auto.

Secondo alcuni in quei giorni Alice Huang potrebbe aver cominciato a usare la sua influenza sul capo della Nvidia per accedere a informazioni riservate dell’azienda e avere influenzato le sue scelte per favorire le imprese cinesi affamate di processori.

Da tempo Jensen Huang è contrario al divieto di vendere i processori più avanzati alla Cina e dopo il ritorno di Donald Trump alla Casa Bianca è riuscito anche a ottenere un allentamento delle norme .

Alla fine del 2024, scrive il New York Times , il dipartimento del commercio degli Stati Uniti aveva aperto un’inchiesta per capire se la Megaspeed faceva arrivare illegalmente processori della Nvidia in Cina. Era finita sotto la lente d’ingrandimento, tra l’altro, una fitta rete di “aziende fantasma” che secondo gli inquirenti serviva a “contrabbandare” i chip.

All’epoca, tuttavia, le indagini si erano bloccate dopo pochi mesi: secondo il quotidiano statunitense potrebbe avere avuto un peso l’influenza che Jensen Huang aveva su Trump e sul segretario al commercio Howard Lutnick.

Ora il dipartimento di giustizia ha deciso di tornare a indagare, sospettando che Huang sia stato al centro di un’operazione dei servizi segreti cinesi, orchestrata grazie alle informazioni fornite da Alice Huang. Il caso rischia di mandare in crisi un’azienda che vale 4.300 miliardi di dollari e mettere in imbarazzo l’amministrazione Trump e la sua strategia per contrastare l’ascesa cinese nel campo dell’ia.

Il 9 novembre Trump ha fatto sapere di aver appreso solo di recente dei sospetti su Huang e che l’Fbi indagherà per andare a fondo alla vicenda. Ma il Financial Times scrive che già maggio, prima della visita di Trump in Cina, il segretario di stato Marco Rubio aveva preso visione di un rapporto riservato sulla relazione del capo della Nvidia con una sospetta spia cinese. Inizialmente Huang, che accompagna regolarmente Trump in ogni visita importante, era stato escluso dal viaggio in Cina, ma poi si era imbarcato sull’Air Force One in Alaska .

Questa vicenda degna di un film di spionaggio girato a Hollywood, tuttavia, può essere letta anche su un altro piano: il caso di Jensen Huang dimostra ancora una volta gli effetti negativi di multinazionali, soprattutto quelle del settore tecnologico, che legano il proprio destino ai loro manager.

In altre multinazionali come Boeing, McDonald’s, Bp o Nestlé sono stati licenziati amministratori delegati che avevano relazioni sentimentali con persone della stessa azienda, perché questo violava le regole interne. Ma in quei casi evidentemente non si trattava di superstar che avevano costruito dal nulla dei colossi.

Come avviene in politica – e il caso di Donald Trump lo dimostra chiaramente – anche in un’azienda pensare che una sorta di “dittatura a fin di bene” dell’uomo forte possa produrre risultati eccezionali è un’illusione: prima o poi, infatti, il dittatore smette di essere benevolo e si scopre che fa danni enormi. ◆

Internazionale pubblica ogni settimana una pagina di lettere. Ci piacerebbe sapere cosa pensi di questo articolo. Scrivici a: posta@internazionale.it

items.title: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave
items.summary: Nine members of the political dynasty say the 250ft structure would cast a shadow on gravesites.
items.content:
The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.

Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.

The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery".

"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC.

"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.

Last week the project won approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

But US District Judge Tanya Chutkan then ruled there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch as litigation plays out.

The Kennedy family filed its complaint under a joint lawsuit brought by the state of Virginia and Washington DC seeking to block construction, arguing that the arch will damage "historically significant sightlines" if erected at the gateway of the cemetery.

The plaintiffs include seven children of Robert and Ethel Kennedy, as well as their grandson - former Democrat congressman Joe Kennedy - and Ted Kennedy's son Edward Kennedy Jr.

It does not include Trump cabinet official Robert F Kennedy Jr, who leads the Department of Health and Human Services.

Their motion moves to intervene in two other lawsuits filed by conservationists and veterans seeking to halt the construction.

They say the arch would be a "permanent denigration" of the gravesites and that the Kennedy offspring "would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended".

The Kennedy family argues the structure "will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family's honor" at the cemetery.

The structure would also "fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites", including the memorials of hundreds of thousands of US veterans, the Kennedys said.

The complaint said that the National Park Service and Interior Department authorised construction on 5 November 2026 without the necessary congressional approval.

The so-called Arc de Trump is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.

Last year, he also added his name to the Kennedy Center, a major Washington DC cultural institution named in honour of JFK.

Trump's name remained on the facade for six months until the addition was ruled illegal and removed.

Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument

items.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
items.summary: The 82-year-old was placed under house detention in Florida last week after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
items.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.

FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Meghan joins Harry in Brussels in first public appearance since father's arrest

Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge

Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices

items.title: A great old-timey game-programming hack (2013)
items.summary: Article URL: https://blog.moertel.com/posts/2013-12-14-great-old-timey-game-programming-hack.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50448921 Points: 219 # Comments: 46
items.content:
A long time ago, when I was a college undergrad, I spent some time working on computer video games. This was in the 8-bit PC era, when the gaming hardware was almost impossibly slow by today’s standards.

It might not surprise you, then, to learn that game programmers of yore did all sorts of crazy things to make their games run at playable speeds. Crazy, crazy things.

While I’ve done my best to recall the important details, I may have gotten some things wrong. If I have, please forgive me. It was a long time ago.

( Note: This post contains some small images as inline-data URLs that some feed readers apparently don’t handle well. If you can’t see the images in your feed, click through to the original article to see them. )

Update 2013-12-16: There have been lots of great comments about this story on Hacker News and Proggit , as well as here on the blog . Thanks for sharing, everyone!

A friend of mine, a gifted programmer, was nearly finished with a new game. Somehow, he had squeezed into a 1980’s-era PC, pretty faithfully, what was at the time a graphically impressive coin-op game popular at the arcades.

The only problem was that his version of the game was unplayable. It was too slow, and the choppy motion broke the player’s immersion. It was after all a side-scroller.

My friend, who had been working on the game while also taking a full load of college courses, was starting to seem a little frazzled. Fearing that he had missed some easy optimization, he asked me to take a look at the code.

The code was tight . Everywhere I looked, he had already done all the things I could think of. Loops had been unrolled. Unneeded draws had been eliminated. All evidence of waste had vanished.

Before I get to the crazy stuff, however, I should back up and explain how graphics hardware worked back then.

Here’s the quick version: The graphics hardware didn’t do jack squat.

On the PC in question, if you wanted to draw something onto the screen, you had to do that yourself, byte by byte. No texture mappers, no blitters. Just bytes. Bytes that you had to move yourself.

My friend’s game spent most of its time redrawing the background. (Again: side-scroller.) For every frame, it had to draw nearly a screen’s worth of background tiles, shifted for the player’s position.

If my memory serves me, each tile was 28 by 28 pixels. Each pixel was one of 16 colors, taking half a byte to represent. Therefore, tiles were represented in memory as 28 contiguous rows of 14 bytes each. The first 14 bytes represented the first row, the second 14 bytes the second row, and so on.

The screen, however, was 320 pixels wide by 240 pixels high. In memory, then, a screen buffer was laid out as 240 contiguous rows of 160 bytes each.

So when copying a tile at address X onto a screen buffer location starting at address Y , you had to copy 28 rows. To copy each row, you had to copy 14 bytes. Fortunately, the processor for this game was a 6809, which had a few 16-bit index registers and delightful “auto-increment” addressing modes (sort of like applying the postfix ++ operator to pointers in C). That meant you could copy 4 pixels at a time while advancing both the X and Y registers in passing:

To copy a full row, you had to do that seven times, so you might sandwich those lines within a 7-count loop:

When you were done copying the row, you needed to advance the destination pointer Y so that it pointed to the starting address for the next row you would draw into the screen buffer. Since the screen buffer was 160 bytes wide and a tile was only 14 bytes wide, that meant you had to add their difference to Y :

That’s one. To copy a full tile, you need to do the same thing 28 times. So, in turn, you sandwich that code within a 28-count loop.

Putting it all together, and giving names to the important numbers, you might end up with a subroutine like this:

Knowing that the game is probably going to spend most of its time running that code, you do what any good programmer would: start counting cycles. Here’s the inner loop again, with setup and finishing, annotated with cycle counts:

Looking at those counts within the loop, you’re not likely to miss that you’re burning 21 cycles to copy just 4 pixels. To copy a full row, then, works out to 2 cycles + (7 iterations) * (21 cycles/iteration) + 8 cycles = 157 cycles. Ouch.

But this isn’t your first time at the keyboard. You know what to do. Unroll that loop!

Now, with the loop overhead reduced to zero – you’ve even eliminated the set-up – each row takes only 7 * (8 + 8) + 8 = 120 cycles. That’s a 30-percent speed-up. Pretty good.

And that’s where most programmers probably would have left it.

He knew that those ++ operations were costly, 3 cycles apiece. And, with the loop unrolled, he also knew exactly where each word to be read or written was located with respect to X or Y . So he cleverly replaced those 3-cycle post-increments with exact offsets. They cost only 1 cycle apiece, and the 0 offset is actually free:

With his optimizations, the cycle count per row had been reduced to (5 + 5) + 6 * (6 + 6) + (8 + 8) = 98 cycles. Compared to the original code, that’s 60 percent faster:

Putting it all together – and, again, I’m going by memory so the code might have been slightly different – the copy-tile subroutine looked something like this, and it copied a full tile, all 28 rows, in a lean 2893 cycles:

This code, all in all, was 60% faster than the naive COPYTILE code we started out with.

So when my friend showed me his code and asked if I could make it faster, I really wanted to help him. I really wanted to be able to answer yes.

But I had to answer no. I hated giving that answer. But, studying the code, I couldn’t see any way to speed it up.

Later, I couldn’t get the problem out of my head. Maybe I had missed something. I had grown up on Apple II computers and their 6502 processors. My friend’s code, however, was for the 6809. Maybe it afforded optimizations that I didn’t know about.

With renewing optimism, I dialed into the university’s library to access the card catalog. (These were the days before the World Wide Web.) Through a VT220 terminal emulator, I searched for books about the 6809.

There was one. A 6809 microprocessor manual. It was in the engineering library. Luckily, I was an engineering student and had sign-out privileges.

When I got to the engineering library, I found the book right where it was supposed to be, looking a little beat up:

Not bothering to find a chair, I flipped through the pages standing, looking for some oddball, 6809-specific instruction that might throw a lot of bytes and throw them fast. Page after page, though, turned up nothing.

Then I came upon PSHS . “Push registers on the hardware stack.”

On my beloved 6502, if you wanted to save registers on the stack, you had to do it one register at a time and, even then, by transferring them through the accumulator. It was slow and expensive. So I had learned to avoid the stack when speed mattered.

But on the 6809 you could save all of the registers – or any subset of them – with a single instruction . And, amazingly, it cost a mere 5 cycles, plus 1 cycle more per byte pushed.

Since the processor had three 16-bit general-purpose registers – D , X , and Y – I could load them up and then use a single PSHS instruction to write 6 bytes in just 11 cycles. The corresponding pull instruction, PULS , had the same low cost.

Further, the 6809 had two stack registers, S and U . I could use one as a source pointer and the other as a destination pointer. In theory, with a single PULS / PSHU pair, I could copy 6 bytes in 22 cycles.

Excitement mounting, I headed for the front desk and reached for my student ID. I was going to sign out that wonderful little book for further study.

I would save the S and U registers somewhere, and then point S at the background tile and U at the screen buffer. Then I would pull from S and push to U , copying 6 bytes at a time, using D , X , and Y as go-betweens. To copy the 14 bytes that make up a row would require three such iterations, which unrolled would be about 60 cycles.

When I reached my room, I found a piece of paper and sketched it out:

Just 66 cycles, including the after-row adjustment to U that prepares it for the next row. (Note that the adjustment is now negative.) For comparison, the naive row-copy loop that we looked at earlier took 157 cycles to do the same thing. And my friend’s optimized code took 98. Already, this crazy idea was looking like a big win.

Still, that last PULS / PSHU pair! What a clunker. It was needed to handle the final two bytes per row, since the rows were 28 pixels = 14 bytes wide, and 6 doesn’t divide 14 evenly.

If only the game had used 24-by-24 tiles instead… But it hadn’t, so I pored through the manual, looking for a way to lower the cost of that inevitable last pair.

And then, by surprise, I struck gold! It was another 6809 oddity, the DP register.

On the 6502 and most 8-bit processors of the era, the lowest 256 bytes of memory was called the zero page . The zero page was special because its memory locations had single-byte addresses and could be accessed with shorter and usually faster instructions.

items.title: 'They will kill you too': Sonia Gandhi's turbulent journey in Indian politics
items.summary: Sonia Gandhi's memoir revisits love, loss and political inheritance, offering a deeply personal defence of her family and its legacy.
items.content:
On the morning of 31 October 1984, Sonia Gandhi was a young wife and mother, living in the prime minister's residence in Delhi. She was about to take a bath when she heard shots ring out in the garden.

Her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, India's prime minister, had just left for her office in an adjoining building. Moments later, she would be assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards, in retaliation for the Indian army's storming of the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Sikhism's holiest shrine, earlier that year.

The sound was like firecrackers, but "different". The children's nanny came pounding on the bathroom door, hysterical, pointing towards the garden.

Sonia ran towards the path. A white Ambassador car was moving slowly towards her. Inside, Indira lay covered in blood, her sari stained, her eyes open, her face wearing what Sonia remembered as a look of surprise.

"Mummy, Mummy," she tried to say. No words came. At the hospital, she waited for hours before a doctor's shake of the head told her what she feared.

The ordeal did not end there. Rajiv Gandhi, her husband and the elder son of Indira Gandhi, summoned from a rally in West Bengal, arrived to tell her that party leaders wanted him to become prime minister.

Sonia's response was fury and terror. "They will kill you; they will kill you, too!" she pleaded. Rajiv replied: "They will kill me anyway." That evening, as Indira's body lay at home, Rajiv was sworn in.

It is one of the most searing passages in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's new memoir: private devastation unfolding alongside the pressures of public life.

The woman who had largely stayed away from politics was now married to India's prime minister, and would eventually find herself at the head of the Congress party, leading it through two general election victories and becoming one of the country's most consequential political figures.

The passage also foreshadows another devastating loss. In 1991, Rajiv himself was assassinated.

At 19, a young woman from a small Italian town, she had met Rajiv, an Indian student, in England. Their relationship took her into a new country and family, and a close bond with Indira followed. India became home through her husband and her mother-in-law.

After Rajiv's killing, even the public appearances required by the memorial trusts she headed became an ordeal. Before speeches, she feared tears would overwhelm her.

When the Dalai Lama asked whether she felt vengeful towards her husband's killers, she answered, "No, I don't," and burst into sobs. Slowly, she writes, Rajiv became "a presence within me rather than a piercing absence".

But grief returned at family milestones. At her son Rahul's Cambridge graduation in 1995, she and her children were overcome by the thought of how proud Rajiv would have been.

Politics, meanwhile, was closing in. The Congress party, the political vehicle of her husband's family for generations, was losing cohesion and electoral ground. Senior leaders were defecting, and the calls for Sonia to step in were growing louder.

She initially refused. She writes she had seen politics through Rajiv: its achievements, but also its "ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery". "I'd always disliked politics," she writes. It had taken first her mother-in-law, then "the love of my life, my children's father".

Yet the party's decline began to feel personal. Walking past photographs of Indira and Rajiv, she was seized by "a mixture of pain and guilt". She feared that the forces they had fought to "protect India's pluralistic ethos" were gaining ground: a rising Hindu nationalism that, in her view, threatened the "secular and pluralistic vision" of India they had sought to defend.

Congress leaders argued that without her, the party could splinter, leaving little to resist communal politics. The family name, she believed, carried an appeal beyond religion, caste, language and region. This, she says, was "the most compelling argument".

Her doubts were also about her own credentials. How could an outsider occupy a position held by two formidable figures? At home, Rahul and Priyanka feared losing their mother as they had lost their grandmother and father. Before a New Year holiday, they extracted a promise: "Don't you do anything crazy while we're away."

The "answer", she says, came through the Bhagavad Gita . Though not religious in adult life, Sonia arranged private lessons with a Sanskrit scholar in January 1997. They read the text verse by verse. She writes that its central message – to perform one's dharma, or duty, without attachment to the fruits of one's actions – eventually resolved her inner conflict.

"I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did."

The memoir's most dramatic political scene, however, comes seven years later, after Congress's 2004 election victory . Sonia had led the party's campaign.

Sonia goes with Manmohan Sing h to meet India's president at the presidential palace in Delhi and formally stake the Congress-led alliance's claim to form a government. Everyone assumes she will become prime minister. She says nothing.

At home, she tells a senior aide she intends to refuse. Party workers gather at the gates; senior colleagues demand a meeting.

"You fought the election, you led us," says one. "People believed in you. How can you let them down like this? Our workers will revolt. You think they'll accept another leader?"

Alliance leaders arrive to persuade her. They surround her, she recalls, and one insists: "We will not take no for an answer." Overwhelmed, she murmurs " Theek hai " - all right. They take it as consent and begin congratulating her.

Her children are appalled, she writes. Rahul storms in: "You said yes?" Her daughter Priyanka urges her not to be forced into a decision.

Sonia writes she spends a long night arguing with herself, friends and family. The risk is not merely personal. She believes the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would continue to exploit her foreign birth and that accepting office would allow the controversy to "create havoc" and hurt the country. By morning she is clear. " I've made up my mind . I'm going to stick to my stand," she tells Rahul.

She chooses Singh, a trained economist and a party member, instead, describing him as a man "above reproach", with a "deep and consummate understanding of governance".

The book is at its most revealing when it turns from family memory to the India she believes has been lost.

Sonia says that when she entered public life there was "a certain decency and decorum in parliamentary politics".

Political attacks and harsh words were not new, but she sees a sharper appetite among those in power "to belittle and torment those who differ from them, to intimidate those they perceive as opponents". It is, she says, part of a wider international drift towards "a heartlessness that accompanies authoritarian regimes".

Her portrait of prime minister Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP is unusually direct.

The two have had "practically no real contact", she writes, beyond formal greetings at parliamentary gatherings and occasional exchanges - " Theek hain, aap ?" ("Are you all right?") - when she returned from hospital. "He tends to look away," she says, "avoiding eye contact."

Modi's idea of India, she writes, was shaped by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and "affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others". His is an India of "hierarchy, order, and control"; hers is "an India against hegemony", standing for "inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice".

There is a striking concession amid the polemic - she says she understood Modi's "discomfort with the ruling elite of our times".

Sonia says she felt uneasy in Delhi's privileged drawing rooms, where political conversation seemed "very far removed from the reality of India".

Modi's origins, she writes, "may not be as humble as his PR team" suggests, but he "had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world". It is a rare acknowledgement of the social distance between the Congress establishment and the electorate Modi came to represent.

The memoir also offers some glimpses of Sonia's encounters with world leaders.

She remembers Vladimir Putin as an "engaging personality" who took her on a boat ride in St Petersburg, pointing out monuments along the way. She says she was impressed by his grasp of geopolitics and his "determination to restore Russia to its former powerful status" - "long before the Ukraine war, a different era".

A more amusing encounter involved France's Nicolas Sarkozy, who arrived in India in 2008 without his then partner Carla Bruni because they were unmarried.

At a state banquet, the Indian vice-president's wife cheerfully grilled him about when he planned to marry her, whether he missed her and whether a date had been fixed. Sarkozy obligingly answered her questions while messaging Bruni on his phone.

Belonging is not a neutral history. The Bofors gun scandal, which badly damaged Rajiv Gandhi's government and dogged the family for decades, gets a relatively brief treatment.

items.title: Vinícius Jr sends message to Sudan boy who received prosthetic legs after BBC report sparks appeal
items.summary: Double amputee Zaher told the BBC last year about his favourite footballer and a dream of being able to walk again.
items.content:
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.

The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.

Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.

We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.

More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.

Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.

More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.

The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.

For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.

When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.

"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.

Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."

Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."

Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.

"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".

Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.

Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.

Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.

"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.

She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."

Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.

Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.

"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time .

There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.

Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.

Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.

After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.

For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.

'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice

Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.

"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."

His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.

As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.

He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.

For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.

The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.

Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine" .

"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.

Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.

Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

Additional reporting by Scarlett Barter and Abdelrahman Abutaleb
